Internship · Mobiclay · Sole designer

Players loved the game, but they had to guess how it worked.

I redesigned a shipped strategy word game to be easy to understand and quick to get around.

  • TeamFounder + developer
  • WhenSummer 2026 · 3 months

120+high-fidelity screens

01The game

One letter is banned

Start your word with any letter of the target except the red one. The rest can be any letters at all, and that's the part players kept missing.

Target word
PLANET

Red is out of play. Every other letter is a way in.

Try a word

Tap a word to play it.

02The problem

The game was fun. Everything around it was scattered.

I spent the first month auditing version 1 end to end with the founder. It surfaced nine problems in four groups.

Scattered

Things that belong together lived apart

  1. 01Coins and subscriptions were bought on unrelated screens.
  2. 02Stats were everywhere: medals in one place, badges in another.
  3. 03Profile and settings were padded with filler.
  4. 04Game modes couldn't sit together without clutter.
Hard to learn

Nothing taught the game well

  1. 05Onboarding took 3 to 5 minutes, couldn't be skipped, and players dropped off before their first game.
  2. 06The rulebook was 17 to 20 pages of text, with no visuals or interaction.
Missing

Key flows didn't exist yet

  1. 07Hosting a game was only hardcoded screens, with no real flow to create one and share it with friends.
  2. 08Wordmine, a new relaxed mode, had no UX at all, and had to stay separate because it isn't competitive.
Discouraging

A good round could still feel like losing

  1. 09One ranking meant “Rank 15 of 18” read as a loss, even after a good round, and rare-word hunters had no way to win.
How might we

Make the whole game easy to understand, in as few taps as possible?

03Structure

Players kept coming back. Home didn't show them where to go.

The founder's brief: reach the rules, see when a new mode opens, keep the leaderboard one tap away. I remapped the app first, then explored 5 home directions.

My first direction had two swipes on one screen. In prototype tests with returning players, they fought each other.

First try

Two swipes became none

Modes became a two-way switch; the carousel became three fixed buttons.

Locked modes stay visible

Craft shows what it takes to unlock, with a progress bar.

Coins live in one place

Packs, ads, plans and history are tabs in Shop, one tap from the coin counter.

04Process

Alternatives, not single answers

The only designer, with the founder and a developer in every review.

1Every flow

Options before decisions

Every flow went to review as two or three working directions. The founder and developer used each, and we chose by comparing pros and cons rather than taste.

2Bigger flows

Prototype tests

Clickable Figma prototypes, shared through the founder with a small group of returning players, to test whether each interaction felt intuitive. This caught the clashing swipes on home.

3The build

Checked on device

Each build tested on a phone for tap targets and legibility, with extra care on small screens. In version 1, the always-open keyboard left no room above it on smaller phones.

05Key solutions

One answer for every problem

01Scattered

Every coin and plan, now in one Shop

Coin packs, ad rewards, plans and transaction history now live in one Shop, with a tab each. It opens from the bottom bar or by tapping the coin counter.

Why this
Why
In version 1, coins and subscriptions were bought on unrelated screens, split between Account and R Coins.
Rejected
Keeping buying inside Account. Players look for money where the coins are.
Trade-off
One screen holds more, so it splits into three tabs: Coin packs, Subscriptions, Transactions.
02Hard to learn

Teach the rule by using it

Short steps that point at the screen, then hand over the keyboard. You're playing by step 5.

Why this
Why
Reading didn't teach the rule. Doing it once does.
Rejected
A video or carousel. Still reading.
Trade-off
More steps, so each is one sentence.
Rulebook

From 20 pages to 5 short sections

The 17–20 page rulebook became How to Play: 5 sections that each answer one question, with visuals, opened only when someone needs them.

Why this
Why
Nobody reads 20 pages of text, and the rulebook had no visuals or interaction.
Rejected
Trimming the same long page. It was still one wall of text.
Trade-off
Rules are split across sections, so each one gets a clear title to find it fast.
03Missing flows

Hosting, built end to end

The hardcoded screens became a real flow: create a game, share a link in one tap, play, then watch the leaderboard fill.

Why this
Why
Hosting existed only as hardcoded screens, so friends had no way to actually play together.
Rejected
Sharing a room code to type in. A link opens the game directly.
Trade-off
More screens to build, so each step does one job.
04Missing flows

Wordmine, a calm space of its own

A relaxed mode with no score pressure: browse a word list, then dig into any word. It has its own button on home and its own brown colour.

Why this
Why
Wordmine had no UX at all, and it had to stay separate because it isn't competitive.
Rejected
Folding it into Core or Craft as another mode. That would bring ranks into a mode meant to be calm.
Trade-off
One more place on home, so it sits in the bottom bar instead of beside the main modes.
05Discouraging

More than one way to win

Rank by game score or rarity, then narrow to 7 days or Friends, so a good round always counts for something.

Why this
Why
One ranking told most players they lost, and rare-word hunters had no way to win.
Rejected
More badges on the same single ranking.
Trade-off
Two scores to explain, so each toggle gets a one-line definition.

Colour tells you what you're doing

Version 1 used colour screen by screen. I gave each kind of play one colour, used everywhere it appears.

06Success signals

Success means players get it on their own

Three things I'd check, and how I'd know it worked.

Comprehension

Can a new player explain their score?

I'd sit with five first-time players, let them finish a round, and ask them to talk me through the score screen. It works if they can name medal and rarity points without any help.

Efficiency

Is it faster to get around?

The same three tasks (play, host, buy coins) on a v1 and a v2 prototype. I'd count taps and time on each. Success is fewer of both in v2.

Retention

Does a low rank still feel okay?

After launch, I'd compare next-day return for players who finish in the bottom half against the top half. If they come back just as often, a low rank isn't pushing them away.

The first two can run on prototypes before launch. Retention needs the live game.

07Reflection

What being the only designer taught me

Options beat opinions

Working alternatives turned “I don't like it” into “this one feels better”.

Answer where the question is

The fix was never more rules. It was one sentence, in the right place.

Next time

Run sessions myself, include brand-new players, and start from WCAG.
